paras: The lynching of Henry Johnson took place at Lake Village, Chicot County, Arkansas, on November 3, 1903, when a white crowd broke into the jail, took Johnson, a Black prisoner, from his cell and hanged him in the center of town. Johnson had been arrested after an early-morning saloon shooting in which Frank Anderson, a white man, was killed. The Associated Press reported it nationally as a "race riot" followed by a lynching, and the New York Sun called Johnson innocent, while papers near the scene held him responsible.

The shooting took place between 1 and 2 a.m. in a saloon owned by Joe Frame, who was also city marshal. Arkansas reports said Anderson objected to Black waiters throwing beer and using profane language, after which, "it is claimed," Ed Coleman, a Black man, drew a pistol and began shooting.

When the fusillade ended, Anderson was dead, B. ("Baldy") Vinson, a Little Rock lawyer, had been shot twice, Frame was wounded in the foot, and Ella McDowell, a Black woman, had been shot in the back. Coleman fled with a posse in pursuit, while Johnson, "one of the negroes in the crowd," made no effort to escape and was jailed.

At noon the courthouse bell rang and most of the white citizens assembled. Speeches were made, a committee on law enforcement was appointed, and it was announced that Circuit Judge Wood would soon hold a special term of court. According to a Little Rock dispatch, "conservative citizens" pleaded for the law to take its course and raised money to prosecute the accused. Instead, a large number rushed out shouting "Hang him!" and, with sledge hammers and railroad irons, broke down four jail doors within thirty minutes.

The mob hanged Johnson in the center of town by the lake front without firing a shot, and his body hung for several hours before the coroner cut it down. Sheriff Frank Strong was in Little Rock at the time.

The town was quiet the next day, and Vinson, whose wounds were first feared fatal, recovered. Ella McDowell died of her wound on the night of November 4. Frame resigned as marshal, and the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic reported that "the people are determined to rid the city of objectionable characters." Coleman was not found, and in December the governor offered a $100 reward for his arrest. No report of an inquest verdict, grand jury inquiry or arrest of any lyncher appears in the coverage.

The AP dispatch ran on November 4 in a fuller version listing the dead and wounded and a shorter one saying the meeting urged "observation of law" before "the more excitable" stormed the jail. Headlines ranged from "Lynching Follows Race Riot" in the Raleigh News & Observer to "Negro Lynched for Being Near a Fight" in the Saint Paul Globe and "Mob Lynches an Innocent Negro" in the Sun. The Montgomery Advertiser, printing a Little Rock Gazette special, headed it "Mightier Than Law."

Closer to the scene, the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic called Johnson and Coleman "responsible," and the Chicot County Life, reprinted in the Greenville (Miss.) Times, called the shooting "entirely unprovoked" and Johnson "the brute." A Little Rock dispatch carried by the Forrest City Times, the Van Buren Press and the Malvern Times-Journal assured readers there was "no fear of further trouble as all the officers are white men." Within days the event shrank to a line in news summaries.
The only Black-press coverage found is the Richmond Planet of November 7, which reprinted the shorter AP text, including the claim that Coleman began the shooting, without headline or comment.

Accounts differ on Johnson's role. The wire called him one of the Black men present, and the Sun said he was "not responsible for the shooting." The Chicot County Life, however, reported Vinson's statement that he saw Johnson fire the fatal shot, and a December item called Johnson "implicated with Coleman" while naming Coleman as the man "who killed F. W. Anderson." The local weekly also put the hanging at about 2 p.m. at a tree at "Bailey's corner," against the noon time in other reports.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: A row between whites and Blacks; 'it is claimed' Coleman began shooting; Johnson, 'one of the negroes in the crowd', was jailed; a courthouse meeting urged law and heard of a special term, but a large number rushed out, broke four jail doors and hanged him at noon.

accounts.label: Little Rock dispatch
accounts.gist: Shooting in a saloon between Black waiters and whites after Anderson resented remarks; Coleman fired first; conservative citizens pleaded and raised money for prosecution; the mob hanged Johnson at the lake front without firing a shot and the body hung for hours.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff Daily Graphic (Dermott report)
accounts.gist: Johnson and Coleman 'are responsible' for Anderson's death; Johnson made no effort to escape and was arrested.

accounts.label: Chicot County Life (local weekly)
accounts.gist: The shooting was 'entirely unprovoked'; Vinson says he saw Johnson fire the fatal shot; a committee of citizens decided to hang him, and he was hanged to a tree at Bailey's corner about 2 p.m.

accounts.label: New York Sun
accounts.gist: A mob of white citizens lynched a Black man 'though not responsible for the shooting.'

framing.detail: AP text ran under headlines such as 'Lynching Follows Race Riot' and 'Negro Hanged in Centre of Town', presenting the 'claimed' wire account.
The New York Sun headed its brief 'Mob Lynches an Innocent Negro.'
Headlines 'Negro Lynched for Being Near a Fight' (Saint Paul Globe) and 'Mightier Than Law' (Montgomery Advertiser) stressed the absence of guilt or the defiance of a promised court.
The Chicot County Life called the shooting 'entirely unprovoked', named Johnson as the shooter and called him 'the brute'; the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic called him 'responsible.'
The Little Rock dispatch reported the lynching plainly and closed with assurance that 'all the officers are white men.'
The Richmond Planet ran the shorter AP text without headline or comment.
